title: Simeliberg
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 142. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, that). The 1857 edition prints this tale without paragraph breaks; the paragraphing here is editorial, added for readability. The wording is unchanged.
about: KHM 142 sends a poor grain-dealer to spy on twelve robbers who open a mountain with the call "Berg Semsi, thu dich auf" and vanish inside with their loot; he learns the password, helps himself to their treasure, and prospers — but his rich, envious brother borrows the trick, gets the name wrong at the crucial moment, and is trapped inside when the robbers return. Simeliberg is the mountain's own name, kept as printed rather than translated.

sentences.t: Es waren zwei Brüder, einer war reich, der andere arm.
sentences.l: There were two brothers, one was rich, the other poor.
sentences.n: reich and arm are adjectives here; the shared glossary answers these two spellings with the nouns das Reich, realm, and der Arm, arm, and both entries are corrected for this tale. Where this tale is broken into paragraphs, the breaks are a modern convenience — the 1857 edition prints it from beginning to end without one, and the text between them is untouched.

sentences.t: Der Reiche aber gab dem Armen nichts, und er mußte sich vom Kornhandel kümmerlich ernähren; da gieng es ihm oft so schlecht, daß er für seine Frau und Kinder kein Brot hatte.
sentences.l: The rich one however gave the poor one nothing, and he had to feed himself meagerly from the grain trade; there it went for him often so badly that he had for his wife and children no bread.
sentences.i: But the rich brother gave the poor one nothing, and he had to keep himself wretchedly by dealing in grain; and often things went so badly with him that he had no bread for his wife and children.
sentences.n: der Reiche and dem Armen are adjectives used as nouns, “the rich one”, “the poor one” — German does this where English wants a noun. sich ernähren von is to live off something. es gieng ihm schlecht is impersonal, with the person in the dative: things went badly for him. gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: Einmal fuhr er mit seinem Karren durch den Wald, da erblickte er zur Seite einen großen kahlen Berg,
sentences.l: Once he drove with his cart through the wood, then he caught sight to the side of a great bare mountain,
sentences.i: One day he was driving his cart through the wood when he caught sight, off to one side, of a great bare mountain,
sentences.n: fahren is to go by vehicle — he is driving a cart, not walking. da, “then, at that”, stands first and throws the verb ahead of its subject: erblickte er. kahl of a hill is bare, without trees.

sentences.t: und weil er den noch nie gesehen hatte, hielt er still und betrachtete ihn mit Verwunderung.
sentences.l: and because he had never yet seen it, he held still and looked at it with astonishment.
sentences.i: and because he had never seen it before, he stopped and stood gazing at it in wonder.
sentences.n: den is a demonstrative standing in for the mountain, “that one”. still halten is to come to a stop. The weil-clause sends its verbs to the end, gesehen hatte, and the main clause then opens with its own verb, hielt.

sentences.t: Wie er so stand, sah er zwölf wilde große Männer daher kommen:
sentences.l: As he stood so, he saw twelve wild big men come along:
sentences.i: As he stood there he saw twelve great wild men come along;
sentences.n: wie here is “as, while”, not “how”. daher kommen is to come along toward the watcher. The colon does the work of a semicolon throughout this printing.

sentences.t: weil er nun glaubte das wären Räuber, schob er seinen Karren ins Gebüsch und stieg auf einen Baum und wartete was da geschehen würde.
sentences.l: because he now believed those were robbers, he shoved his cart into the bushes and climbed up a tree and waited what would happen there.
sentences.i: and since he took them for robbers, he pushed his cart into the bushes and climbed a tree and waited to see what would happen.
sentences.n: das wären Räuber is reported thought: the subjunctive wären keeps it as what he supposed, not what the tale asserts. wartete was has no “to see” — German can leave the seeing unsaid. geschehen würde is the past future, “would happen”.

sentences.t: Die zwölf Männer giengen aber vor den Berg und riefen „Berg Semsi, Berg Semsi, thu dich auf.“
sentences.l: The twelve men however went before the mountain and called “Mountain Semsi, Mountain Semsi, open yourself.”
sentences.i: But the twelve men went up before the mountain and cried, “Mount Semsi, Mount Semsi, open.”
sentences.n: sich aufthun is to open of itself; thu is the 1857 spelling of tu, the imperative of thun (modern tun), and dich is its object — the mountain is told to open itself. The formula is chanted, but the 1857 text prints it inside the running prose, not as verse. Semsi is the mountain’s name: hold on to the spelling, because the tale turns on it later.

sentences.t: Alsbald that sich der kahle Berg in der Mitte von einander, und die zwölfe giengen hinein, und wie sie drin waren, schloß er sich zu.
sentences.l: At once the bare mountain did itself apart in the middle, and the twelve went in, and when they were inside, it shut itself to.
sentences.i: At once the bare mountain parted in the middle, and the twelve went in, and when they were inside it closed again.
sentences.n: sich von einander thun, “to do itself apart”, is this tale’s way of saying it split open. die zwölfe is an older inflected numeral used as a noun, “the twelve of them”. drin is a short form of darin, in there — the shared glossary marks this spelling Low German, which it is not in this High German tale. sich zuschließen is to shut itself; the shared entry answers schloß with das Schloß, a castle, and is corrected here.

sentences.t: Über eine kleine Weile aber that er sich wieder auf, und die Männer kamen heraus und trugen schwere Säcke auf den Rücken,
sentences.l: Over a little while however it did itself open again, and the men came out and carried heavy sacks on their backs,
sentences.i: But after a little while it opened again, and the men came out carrying heavy sacks on their backs,
sentences.n: über eine kleine Weile is “after a little while”. den Rücken is singular where English wants a plural — German keeps a body part singular when each person has one of them.

sentences.t: und wie sie alle wieder am Tageslicht waren, sprachen sie „Berg Semsi, Berg Semsi, thu dich zu.“
sentences.l: and when they were all again in the daylight, they said “Mountain Semsi, Mountain Semsi, shut yourself.”
sentences.i: and when they were all back in the daylight they said, “Mount Semsi, Mount Semsi, close.”
sentences.n: The closing formula is the opening one with zu in place of auf — the separable pair aufthun and zuthun that runs through the whole tale. am Tageslicht uses an where English uses “in”.

sentences.t: Da fuhr der Berg zusammen, und war kein Eingang mehr an ihm zu sehen, und die Zwölfe giengen fort.
sentences.l: Then the mountain drew together, and was no entrance any more to be seen on it, and the Twelve went away.
sentences.i: Then the mountain closed up, and no way in was to be seen on it any more, and the twelve went off.
sentences.n: zusammenfahren of a thing is to snap shut; of a person it is to start with fright. The middle clause has no subject at all — German drops es, and the literal keeps the gap. war … zu sehen is “was to be seen”. die Zwölfe is capitalised here: the twelve as a company.

sentences.t: Als sie ihm nun ganz aus den Augen waren, stieg der Arme vom Baum herunter, und war neugierig was wohl im Berge heimliches verborgen wäre.
sentences.l: When they were now quite out of his eyes, the poor one climbed down from the tree, and was curious what secret [thing] might be hidden in the mountain.
sentences.i: When they were quite out of his sight the poor brother climbed down from the tree, curious to know what secret thing might lie hidden in the mountain.
sentences.n: jemandem aus den Augen sein is to be out of someone’s sight, with the person in the dative, ihm. im Berge is the dative singular with an old -e; the shared glossary answers this spelling as a plural and is corrected here. heimliches is an adjective standing alone, so the literal supplies [thing] in square brackets. wohl softens it to “I wonder what”, and wäre keeps it as his supposing.

sentences.t: Also gieng er davor und sprach „Berg Semsi, Berg Semsi, thu dich auf,“ und der Berg that sich auch vor ihm auf.
sentences.l: So he went before it and said “Mountain Semsi, Mountain Semsi, open yourself,” and the mountain did itself open before him too.
sentences.i: So he went up before it and said, “Mount Semsi, Mount Semsi, open,” and the mountain opened for him as well.
sentences.n: also is the old “so, thus”, never English “also”. davor, “before it”, saves naming the mountain again. auch belongs to the whole clause: it opened for him too, as it had for the robbers.

sentences.t: Da trat er hinein, und der ganze Berg war eine Höhle voll Silber und Gold, und hinten lagen große Haufen Perlen und blitzende Edelsteine, wie Korn aufgeschüttet.
sentences.l: Then he stepped in, and the whole mountain was a cave full of silver and gold, and at the back lay great heaps of pearls and flashing precious stones, heaped up like grain.
sentences.i: Then he stepped inside, and the whole mountain was a cavern full of silver and gold, and at the back lay great heaps of pearls and glittering jewels, poured up like grain.
sentences.n: voll takes its noun bare, with no “of”: voll Silber und Gold. aufschütten is to heap or pour up in a pile, as grain is heaped in a loft — the comparison measures the treasure in the poor man’s own trade.

sentences.t: Der Arme wußte gar nicht was er anfangen sollte, und ob er sich etwas von den Schätzen nehmen dürfte;
sentences.l: The poor one did not know at all what he should set about, and whether he might take himself something of the treasures;
sentences.i: The poor brother did not know at all what to do, or whether he might take anything of the treasure for himself;
sentences.n: etwas anfangen is to set about something, to know what to do. dürfte is the subjunctive of dürfen, “might, would be allowed to”, and keeps the question his own. sich nehmen carries the dative of interest, taking for oneself.

sentences.t: endlich füllte er sich die Taschen mit Gold, die Perlen und Edelsteine aber ließ er liegen.
sentences.l: at last he filled himself the pockets with gold, the pearls and precious stones however he let lie.
sentences.i: at last he filled his pockets with gold, but the pearls and jewels he left lying where they were.
sentences.n: sich die Taschen füllen — the dative sich does the work of English “his”. liegen lassen is to leave a thing lying, to let it be. The object stands first for contrast, which puts the subject er behind the verb.

sentences.t: Als er wieder herauskam, sprach er gleichfalls „Berg Semsi, Berg Semsi, thu dich zu,“ da schloß sich der Berg, und er fuhr mit seinem Karren nach Haus.
sentences.l: When he came out again, he said likewise “Mountain Semsi, Mountain Semsi, shut yourself,” then the mountain closed itself, and he drove with his cart home.
sentences.i: When he came out again he said in the same way, “Mount Semsi, Mount Semsi, close,” and the mountain shut, and he drove home with his cart.
sentences.n: gleichfalls is “in the same way, likewise”. nach Haus, without an article, is the fixed phrase for homeward.

sentences.t: Nun brauchte er nicht mehr zu sorgen und konnte mit seinem Golde für Frau und Kind Brot und auch Wein dazu kaufen,
sentences.l: Now he needed no more to worry and could with his gold buy for wife and child bread and also wine to it,
sentences.i: Now he had no more need to worry, and could buy bread with his gold for wife and child, and wine to go with it,
sentences.n: brauchen with nicht and zu is to have no need to. sorgen here is the verb, to worry — the shared glossary answers this spelling with the plural noun die Sorgen and is corrected for this tale. Golde is a dative with the old -e. dazu is “to it, in addition”.

sentences.t: lebte fröhlich und redlich, gab den Armen und that jedermann Gutes.
sentences.l: lived cheerfully and honestly, gave to the poor and did everyone good.
sentences.i: and he lived cheerfully and honestly, gave to the poor, and did good to everyone.
sentences.n: The subject er is not repeated; the sentence runs on from the clause before, and the literal keeps the gap. den Armen is the dative plural of the adjective used as a noun, “to the poor”. jemandem Gutes thun puts the person in the dative.

sentences.t: Als aber das Geld zu Ende war, gieng er zu seinem Bruder, lieh einen Scheffel und holte sich von neuem; doch rührte er von den großen Schätzen nichts an.
sentences.l: But when the money was at an end, he went to his brother, borrowed a bushel-measure and fetched himself anew; yet he touched nothing of the great treasures.
sentences.i: But when the money came to an end he went to his brother, borrowed a bushel measure and fetched himself more; still he laid no hand on the great treasures.
sentences.n: leihen serves both borrowing and lending, and only the sentence says which; here he borrows. der Scheffel is an old dry measure of about a bushel — and the vessel itself, which is what will betray him. von neuem is “afresh”. anrühren is separable, its an waiting at the end: rührte … an.

sentences.t: Wie er sich zum drittenmal etwas holen wollte, borgte er bei seinem Bruder abermals den Scheffel.
sentences.l: When he wanted to fetch himself something for the third time, he borrowed from his brother once again the bushel-measure.
sentences.i: When he wanted to fetch himself something for the third time, he again borrowed the measure from his brother.
sentences.n: borgen bei jemandem is to borrow from someone — bei, where English says “from”. abermals is an older “once again”. zum drittenmal is the count the tale is keeping, and the robbers will keep it too.

sentences.t: Der Reiche war aber schon lange neidisch über sein Vermögen und den schönen Haushalt, den er sich eingerichtet hatte,
sentences.l: The rich one however was already long envious over his property and the fine household that he had set up for himself,
sentences.i: But the rich brother had long been envious of his property and of the fine household he had set up for himself,
sentences.n: neidisch über etwas sein is to be envious of something; modern German prefers auf. schon lange with a past tense is “had long been”. sich einrichten is to set oneself up, to furnish a household.

sentences.t: und konnte nicht begreifen woher der Reichthum käme und was sein Bruder mit dem Scheffel anfienge.
sentences.l: and could not grasp from where the wealth came and what his brother set about with the bushel-measure.
sentences.i: and could not make out where the wealth came from, or what his brother was doing with the measure.
sentences.n: käme and anfienge are subjunctives in an indirect question — the rich brother’s puzzling, not the tale’s statement; anfienge is the 1857 spelling of anfinge. Reichthum keeps the older th, modern Reichtum.

sentences.t: Da dachte er eine List aus und bestrich den Boden mit Pech, und wie er das Maß zurück bekam, so war ein Goldstück darin hängen geblieben.
sentences.l: Then he thought out a ruse and smeared the bottom with pitch, and when he got the measure back, a gold piece had stuck inside it.
sentences.i: So he thought out a trick and smeared the bottom with pitch, and when he got the measure back, a gold piece had stuck fast inside.
sentences.n: eine List ausdenken is separable: dachte … aus. der Boden here is the bottom of the vessel, not the ground. hängen bleiben is to stay hanging, to stick fast, and forms its perfect with sein: war … geblieben.

sentences.t: Alsbald gieng er zu seinem Bruder und fragte ihn „was hast du mit dem Scheffel gemessen?“
sentences.l: At once he went to his brother and asked him “what have you measured with the bushel-measure?”
sentences.i: At once he went to his brother and asked him, “What have you been measuring with the bushel?”
sentences.n: alsbald is an elevated “at once, straightway”. gemessen is the past participle of messen, to measure; das Maß in the sentence before comes from the same root.

sentences.t: „Korn und Gerste“ sagte der andere.
sentences.l: “Grain and barley” said the other.
sentences.i: “Corn and barley,” said the other.
sentences.n: Korn is grain in general, and in the north rye in particular; it is what a grain-dealer would truthfully be measuring, and the answer is a lie all the same. The 1857 text sets no comma before sagte.

sentences.t: Da zeigte er ihm das Goldstück und drohte ihm, wenn er nicht die Wahrheit sagte, so wollt er ihn beim Gericht verklagen.
sentences.l: Then he showed him the gold piece and threatened him, if he did not tell the truth, then he would accuse him before the court.
sentences.i: Then he showed him the gold piece and threatened him: if he did not tell the truth, he would denounce him to the court.
sentences.n: drohen takes the dative, ihm. What follows is reported speech with no daß to introduce it; wollt (for wollte) is the rich brother’s own “I will”, shifted into the past. beim Gericht verklagen is to bring a charge against someone before the court.

sentences.t: Er erzählte ihm nun alles, wie es zugegangen war.
sentences.l: He told him now everything, how it had come about.
sentences.i: So he told him everything, and how it had all come about.
sentences.n: zugehen, of events, is to come to pass, and forms its perfect with sein: war … zugegangen. The second half hangs on erzählte as a second object: he told him how.

sentences.t: Der Reiche aber ließ gleich einen Wagen anspannen, fuhr hinaus, wollte die Gelegenheit besser benutzen und ganz andere Schätze mitbringen.
sentences.l: The rich one however had at once a wagon harnessed, drove out, wanted to use the opportunity better and to bring back quite other treasures.
sentences.i: But the rich brother had a wagon harnessed at once and drove out, meaning to make better use of the chance and to bring back treasures of quite another kind.
sentences.n: lassen with an infinitive is to have something done: ließ … anspannen, had the horses put to. anspannen is to harness a horse to a cart. ganz andere is “quite other”, of a different order altogether — his brother had taken only what fitted in his pockets.

sentences.t: Wie er vor den Berg kam, rief er „Berg Semsi, Berg Semsi, thu dich auf.“
sentences.l: When he came before the mountain, he called “Mountain Semsi, Mountain Semsi, open yourself.”
sentences.i: When he came before the mountain he cried, “Mount Semsi, Mount Semsi, open.”
sentences.n: The formula is word for word the one the robbers used and the one his brother used; the 1857 text prints it identically every time, which is what will make the slip visible when it comes.

sentences.t: Der Berg that sich auf, und er gieng hinein.
sentences.l: The mountain did itself open, and he went in.
sentences.i: The mountain opened, and he went inside.
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat. sich aufthun, to open of itself, is the verb of the chant, now in the past.

sentences.t: Da lagen die Reichthümer alle vor ihm, und er wußte lange nicht wozu er am ersten greifen sollte, endlich lud er Edelsteine auf so viel er tragen konnte.
sentences.l: There lay the riches all before him, and he knew for a long time not to what he should reach first, at last he loaded up precious stones as many as he could carry.
sentences.i: There lay all the riches before him, and for a long while he did not know what to reach for first; at last he loaded up as many jewels as he could carry.
sentences.n: wozu here is plain “to what” — what to reach for; the shared glossary answers this spelling with a quite different sense and is corrected for this tale. greifen nach or zu is to reach for. am ersten is an old superlative adverb, “first of all”. aufladen is separable: lud … auf.

sentences.t: Er wollte seine Last hinausbringen, weil aber Herz und Sinn ganz voll von den Schätzen waren, hatte er darüber den Namen des Berges vergessen und rief „Berg Simeli, Berg Simeli, thu dich auf.“
sentences.l: He wanted to bring his load out, but because heart and mind were quite full of the treasures, he had over it forgotten the name of the mountain and called “Mountain Simeli, Mountain Simeli, open yourself.”
sentences.i: He wanted to carry his load out, but because heart and mind were so full of the treasure, he had forgotten the mountain’s name over it, and cried, “Mount Simeli, Mount Simeli, open.”
sentences.n: This is the hinge of the tale: Simeli is not Semsi. The 1857 text prints both spellings, and the difference of a syllable is what kills him — the tale is even named after the wrong one, Simeliberg. darüber is “over it, in the midst of it”: the treasure crowded the name out. Herz und Sinn stand without articles, as a set pair.

sentences.t: Aber das war der rechte Name nicht, und der Berg regte sich nicht und blieb verschlossen.
sentences.l: But that was the right name not, and the mountain did not stir itself and remained shut.
sentences.i: But that was not the right name, and the mountain did not stir, and stayed shut.
sentences.n: German keeps nicht at the end when a whole phrase is denied: der rechte Name nicht. sich regen is to stir, to move at all — the same verb the devil’s hiding-place uses elsewhere in the book.

sentences.t: Da ward ihm angst, aber je länger er nachsann, desto mehr verwirrten sich seine Gedanken, und halfen ihm alle Schätze nichts mehr.
sentences.l: Then it became fearful to him, but the longer he pondered, the more his thoughts tangled themselves, and all the treasures helped him nothing any more.
sentences.i: Then fear came over him, and the longer he pondered the more his thoughts tangled, and all the treasure was of no more use to him.
sentences.n: ward ihm angst is impersonal with the person in the dative: fear came over him; ward is the old past of werden. je … desto is “the … the”. sich verwirren is to grow confused; the shared glossary answers this spelling as a participle said of tangled flax, and it is corrected here. helfen takes the dative, and nichts is its measure: helped him nothing.

sentences.t: Am Abend that sich der Berg auf und die zwölf Räuber kamen herein,
sentences.l: In the evening the mountain did itself open and the twelve robbers came in,
sentences.i: In the evening the mountain opened and the twelve robbers came in,
sentences.n: am Abend is the fixed phrase for “in the evening”. herein is inward toward where we stand — and we are inside now, with the trapped man; hinein, used earlier, was inward away from us.

sentences.t: und als sie ihn sahen, lachten sie und riefen „Vogel, haben wir dich endlich, meinst du wir hättens nicht gemerkt daß du zweimal hereingekommen bist, aber wir konnten dich nicht fangen, zum drittenmal sollst du nicht wieder heraus.“
sentences.l: and when they saw him, they laughed and called “Bird, have we you at last, do you think we had not noticed that you have come in twice, but we could not catch you, for the third time you shall not get out again.”
sentences.i: and when they saw him they laughed and cried, “Bird, have we got you at last? Do you think we had not noticed that you came in twice? We could not catch you then — this third time you shall not get out again.”
sentences.n: Vogel as an address is a taunt, roughly “my fine bird”, said to a thing caught. haben wir dich endlich is a question by word order alone; the 1857 printing gives it no question mark. hättens is hätten es, and the subjunctive keeps it inside their mockery. The last clause has no verb of motion at all — sollst du nicht wieder heraus, “you shall not out again” — and the going is left unsaid. They are counting visits, and the man they have caught did not make the first two.

sentences.t: Da rief er „ich wars nicht, mein Bruder wars,“ aber er mochte bitten um sein Leben und sagen was er wollte, sie schlugen ihm das Haupt ab.
sentences.l: Then he cried “it was not I, my brother it was,” but he might beg for his life and say what he would, they struck his head off.
sentences.i: Then he cried, “It was not I, it was my brother!” — but beg for his life and say what he would, they struck his head off.
sentences.n: wars is war es, “it was”. er mochte bitten … und sagen was er wollte is the old concessive use of mögen: however much he begged, whatever he said. abschlagen is separable, and its ab falls at the very end of the tale. jemandem das Haupt abschlagen puts the man in the dative, ihm, the head being his; Haupt is the elevated word for head. The tale stops there, and says nothing more of the poor brother.

glossary.anfienge: anfangen — was doing, was up to (3rd sg. subjunctive II; 1857 spelling of anfinge; mit etwas anfangen: to do with something)
glossary.arm: arm — poor (adjective); also der Arm — arm
glossary.arme: der Arme — the poor man (adjective used as a noun); also arme: poor (inflected adjective)
glossary.berge: der Berg — mountain (dat. sg. with old -e: im Berge, in the mountain)
glossary.boden: der Boden — the bottom (of a vessel); also: ground, floor
glossary.drin: drin — in there, inside (colloquial short form of darin; High German, not dialect)
glossary.fuhr: fahren — drove, went (3rd sg. past; of going by cart or carriage; fuhr zusammen: snapped shut)
glossary.reich: reich — rich (adjective); also das Reich — realm, kingdom
glossary.reiche: der Reiche — the rich man (adjective used as a noun); also reiche: I hand, reach, from reichen
glossary.schloß: schließen — shut, closed (3rd sg. past; sich zuschließen: to close up); also das Schloß — castle, lock
glossary.sorgen: sorgen — to worry, take care (infinitive); also die Sorgen — cares, worries
glossary.verwirrten: verwirren — grew confused, tangled (3rd pl. past; sich verwirren: to get into a tangle)
glossary.wollt: wollen — would, wanted (3rd sg. past, shortened wollte; also 2nd pl. present wollt)
glossary.wozu: wozu — to what, for what (wozu greifen: what to reach for)
glossary.zwölfe: zwölf — twelve (older inflected form; die zwölfe: the twelve of them)
